You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.

[Will I get hungry and thirstier during a fast?]

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	Intermittent Fasting Myths
     2	“It’s just starving yourself.”
     3	Fasting is a planned action to avoid food for a set period of time. The body
     4	can still use energy from its own fat stores during a fast, so it isn’t being
     5	deprived. Starvation is completely different. It is unplanned, it doesn’t have a
     6	chosen end point, and the body doesn’t have much stored energy that it can
     7	use. It is simply untrue to say that fasting is the same as starving yourself!
     8	“It will slow your metabolism.”
     9	When someone follows a reduced calorie diet but continues to eat regularly (i.e., “little and
    10	often”), insulin levels remain high for most of the day. This stops the body from using stored
    11	fat for energy. It responds by reducing the amount of calories it burns, to save what energy
    12	it does have (i.e., it slows your metabolism). Fasting is different. During a fast, insulin levels
    13	are reduced, so fat stored in the body can be used for energy. This means that metabolism
    14	does not need to be slowed down, as the body does not think it is being deprived.
    15	“Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.”
    16	In the morning, the body’s releases hormones to get us ready to start the day.
    17	This causes the release of energy from the body’s stores, which means we
    18	don’t actually need to eat something first thing in the morning, as the body is
    19	being fed whether you eat something or not! No meal is more important than
    20	any other. What does matter is that you get all the nutrients you need from
    21	what you do eat.
    22	“You’ll be deprived of essential nutrients.”
    23	As long as a range of real foods are eaten in the non-fasting periods, there is no reason
    24	that people who try intermittent fasting should experience any nutrient deficiencies.
    25	“It’ll make your body break down muscle.”
    26	If available, the body will always use glucose and/or fat for fuel. Your muscles,
    27	and the proteins they are made up of, are only a last resort for this. Studies
    28	have shown that intermittent fasting does not cause significant muscle loss,
    29	and that levels of a growth hormone that protects muscles from being used
    30	for energy are increased during a fast. It is important that sufficient protein
    31	is eaten in the non-fasting periods though in order to support the growth
    32	and maintenance of muscle mass.
    33	“You’ll be hungry all the time and will just eat much more at the next meal.”
    34	Studies have shown that missing a meal may result in slightly more food being eaten at
    35	the next meal, but the total energy intake will still be less than if you had eaten both meals.
    36	Fasting decreases hunger hormones and increases fullness. So although you may feel
    37	hungry when you first try fasting, many people actually report reduced hunger once they
    38	are used to it.
    39	www.xperthealth.org.uk
    40	Stay hydrated
    41	When you eat, you get some water from your food. So during a fast, you
    42	are missing out on some of the fluids you normally get. This can lead to you
    43	becoming dehydrated, causing side effects such as tiredness and headaches.
    44	Dehydration can also be mistaken for hunger, which can make it more difficult
    45	to stick to your planned fast.
    46	The best option for staying hydrated is water. If you want to make it a bit more exciting then
    47	you can flavour it, with a slice of lemon, orange, lime or cucumber for example. Coffee (black or
    48	flavoured with natural extracts), tea (black, green, herbal or fruit), or broth (bone or vegetable)
    49	are all also suitable options.
    50	Stick with it
    51	You may struggle at first if you are not used to going for extended periods of
    52	time without food, but much of this could be down to habit. If you have had
    53	a set routine for a long time your body will expect to receive food at certain
    54	times of the day. So when it doesn’t get the food it is expecting, this can
    55	trigger feelings of hunger. Most people adapt quite quickly though, so find it
    56	increasingly easy to fast. But in the short-term, make sure you have thought about what
    57	you could do to try and distract yourself when you feel hungry.
    58	Break your fast with nutritious foods
    59	At the end of your fast, have a meal that includes plenty of real, minimally
    60	processed food. Make sure this meal includes one or two portions of good
    61	quality protein. This will help to satisfy your appetite, and to make sure your
    62	body gets plenty of nutrients. Planning a meal that supports your dietary
    63	approach but also includes some of your favourite foods to break your fast with can help to
    64	motivate you to stick with it too.
    65	Make sure you get enough salt
    66	People often think salt is unhealthy, but we do need some in our diet. Sodium is an
    67	essential nutrient, and the main source of it is salt. When you are not eating (i.e.,
    68	during a fast), you are not taking in any salt. On top of this, the reduction in insulin
    69	levels during fasting results in less salt being held in the blood. Signs of having
    70	low sodium levels include dizziness (caused by a drop in blood pressure), muscle
    71	cramps, headaches and tiredness. These symptoms can be fixed by making sure
    72	you get enough salt and water. Salt can be added to meals in non-fasting periods, or you
    73	can get more by having salted water or bone broth during fasting periods.
    74	Don’t worry if you regain a bit of weight after a fast
    75	When you fast you will lose weight because your body is using up some of your
    76	stored fat for fuel. But you will also lose some weight for other reasons, including
    77	that there will be less food and waste passing through your body. This means
    78	that when you break your fast you might actually regain a little bit of weight. This
    79	is completely normal though, so you should not feel disappointed. The good news
    80	is that you will still have reduced the amount of fat stored in your body!

Based on `doc.txt`:

**Hunger**
- You may feel hungry when you first try fasting, and you may struggle at first if you're not used to going for extended periods without food. Much of this could be down to habit: if you've had a set routine for a long time, your body expects food at certain times, and not getting it can trigger feelings of hunger.
- However, fasting decreases hunger hormones and increases fullness, so many people actually report reduced hunger once they are used to it. Most people adapt quite quickly and find it increasingly easy to fast.
- Missing a meal may result in slightly more food being eaten at the next meal, but total energy intake will still be less than if you had eaten both meals.

**Thirst / hydration**
- The document doesn't say you will become thirstier, but it notes that when you eat, you get some water from your food, so during a fast you are missing out on some of the fluids you normally get. This can lead to dehydration, causing side effects such as tiredness and headaches, and dehydration can also be mistaken for hunger, making it harder to stick to the fast.
- To stay hydrated, the best option is water (which can be flavoured with a slice of lemon, orange, lime or cucumber); coffee (black or flavoured with natural extracts), tea (black, green, herbal or fruit), or broth (bone or vegetable) are also suitable options.
